articles.title: A Practical JSON Debugging Checklist: 4 Common Errors and How to Fix Them
articles.excerpt: A Practical JSON Debugging Checklist: 4 Common Errors and How to Fix Them JSON is easy to read and write, but a tiny syntax mistake can make an entire API response or configuration file impossible to…
articles.body: A Practical JSON Debugging Checklist: 4 Common Errors and How to Fix Them JSON is easy to read and write, but a tiny syntax mistake can make an entire API response or configuration file impossible to parse. When JSON.parse() throws an error, the problem is often one of a few common mistakes. Here are four issues worth checking before spending time debugging your application. 1. Trailing Commas JSON does not allow a comma after the last property in an object or the last element in an array. Incorrect: { "name" : "Alex" , "role" : "Developer" , } Correct: { "name" : "Alex" , "role" : "Developer" } This mistake is especially common when copying JavaScript objects into a JSON file. JavaScript object literals may allow trailing commas, but standard JSON does not. 2.

articles.title: What AI makes you learn
articles.excerpt: Ask a language model to pick a random number between 1 and 10. I did it 900 times, with nine Claude and GPT models, and all 900 times the answer was 7. Ask for one between 1 and 100 and each model has…
articles.body: Ask a language model to pick a random number between 1 and 10. I did it 900 times, with nine Claude and GPT models, and all 900 times the answer was 7. Ask for one between 1 and 100 and each model has its favourite: in some tests across several models , ChatGPT settled on 47, Claude 3 Haiku on 42 and Gemini on 72. A 2025 study puts it down to biases in the data they were trained on. It isn't a curious glitch. It's the simplest way to see how the thing works inside, and it explains almost everything I described in Oracle or tool : why the first answer is the conventional one, why definitions drift towards popular usage. There I argued that using AI doesn't require knowing everything, only having a method.

articles.title: RAG evaluation: how do you test that citations hold up?
articles.excerpt: A citation that does not support its claim is worse than no citation, because it looks like proof. This piece shows how we test cited answers claim by claim: retrieval kept apart from generation, supp…
articles.body: A citation that does not support its claim is worse than no citation, because it looks like proof. This piece shows how we test cited answers claim by claim: retrieval kept apart from generation, support scored against the exact passage each claim cites, and the cases that break trust, from questions the documents do not answer to passages the user is not allowed to see. A wrong citation is not a small error. It is a false receipt. Short answer Good RAG evaluation tests citations claim by claim. Split each answer into its individual claims, check every claim against the exact passage it cites, and score support, not presence. Then test the cases that break trust: questions the documents do not answer, near-identical names, lists and tables, and passages the user is not allowed to see.

articles.body: Gemini 4 Carbon is Argon with more thinking per turn. Google documents native long decode up to 1,048,576 tokens minus input, while AIHubMix currently documents only Chat Completions; keep gateway requests at or below 65,536. Google charges the same introductory rate ($2/M input, $10/M output through November 30, 2026; $4/$20 from December 1), but Carbon spends more tokens and waits longer before its first answer. For queue-based coding agents, the trade can pay off. Artificial Analysis's 2026-11-11T05:23Z snapshot measured Carbon High at 60.03 (#4 of 104), $7.76 per task and 25.6 minutes, versus Argon High at 50.41, $9.95 and 29.0 minutes. First token was slower: 67.1 seconds versus 40.1. What changes in an Argon migration Carbon is based on Argon. The model ID is gemini-4-carbon .

articles.title: From Code to Motor: Why Software Audit Sidecars Fail in Embodied AI
articles.excerpt: In the digital realm, we have tools to catch "false completions" from LLM agents. We use software sidecars to record independent physical witnesses (like file hashes or git diffs) and output four-valu…
articles.body: In the digital realm, we have tools to catch "false completions" from LLM agents. We use software sidecars to record independent physical witnesses (like file hashes or git diffs) and output four-valued verdicts: PASS, FAIL, INVALID, NOT_RUN. But what happens when the agent is not writing code, but controlling a drone or a robot? Recently, I formalized the structural faults that occur when we move digital audits into embodied systems. The core issue is simple: A software exception can roll back a file write, but it cannot roll back a crash. When a software audit sidecar is applied to physical agents, it faces three structural faults: Fault I: Shared-scheduler refusal If the sidecar shares the same CPU and fault domain as the flight controller, it dies when the controller deadlocks.

articles.body: For a while it was the NES . I’d shoot ducks until I got bored, and I hated Mario because it was too hard. What I really remember fondly was watching Mémère play The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past after she upgraded to the SNES. She’d tell me who she was fighting and why, and following along felt like having one of my favorite people read me a book. When it was my turn to play, I’d just charge up Link’s sword and mow every blade of grass I could find. Then I’d go looking for chickens. Then I’d ask what she had for snacks. She always had good snacks for me.

articles.body: A new NASA space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility. The Ultraviolet Explorer (UVEX) mission, developed by NASA in conjunction with the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), will be the first mission to create deep all-sky maps in ultraviolet light. Thus, when it launches in 2031, UVEX will join new sky-mapping surveys like NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer), which scans the cosmos in infrared, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which does the same over the southern hemisphere in visible light, in creating deep-sky maps across a broad swathe of the electromagnetic spectrum.

articles.body: I’ve used several smart telescopes over the last few years, but I'd recommend the ZWO Seestar S30 Plus to almost anyone wanting to get started in astrophotography. At $499/€499, it’s a complete imaging system that can photograph galaxies, nebulae and star clusters automatically, even from a light-polluted city. Better still, it’s so small that it can live on a bookshelf. The Pleiades (M45), photographed in mosaic mode with the Seestar S30 Plus.
